Notes


    
Server rows

    
    
      
  • Badges align with the first line of the name. Every row is now name, address, then one extra line if there is anything to say — the failure on Old 4080, the key warning on Overnight box — so nothing shifts between rows.
    • 
      
  • Set up is gone from the row. You were right that it read as "this needs setting up". Clicking the row opens the server, where Files and Set up are tabs.
    • 
      
  • The three dots open the same menu as a right-click — try it. Five menus, one per shape a server can be in.
    • 
      
  • Smoozy on a server follows the app’s own version, and is updated when Smoozy connects and nothing is running there. The state Smoozy on a server older or newer than the app shows the six lines for when that is not the ordinary case: waiting for its jobs, with Update now…; updating; could not be updated; too old, with jobs that can’t be stopped from here; too old, where Smoozy can’t tell whether it has jobs; too new. None of them says the service isn’t responding, because it is answering, or would be. Update now… asks first, in the removal box’s own words for stop and clear, because stopping and clearing is the only way to replace Smoozy there without ending a render under it. On the ruling of 2026-09-28 that carried the Creator’s no updating while jobs run across to servers.
    • 
    


    
Server badges

    
Every server gets a colour when it is added, and keeps it. It means nothing but which server — it never changes with state. Eight hues 45 degrees apart, around the whole wheel, with red and green among them. A badge is a squircle and every state in Smoozy is a circle, so the shape says which it is before the colour is read.

    
It appears wherever that server does: the rail, the server list, the server's own page, the queue group headings, the history rows, the transfer rows. So a job in history is placed without reading its name.

    
State moved off the circle entirely. Connection is the button — green filled when connected, hollow when not, amber while reconnecting, red and unavailable when it needs a key. In the rail, where there is no room for a button, a server that is not connected simply reads dim. Work is the words in the middle column. The rail's one dot is the exception, on the Creator's word of 2026-10-04: green while a server is connected and idle, amber and pulsing while a job renders on it, none while it is not connected. It replaced the mark that said a panel was open, which the panel's own strip already says.

    
The colour arrives already picked: Smoozy takes the first of the eight nobody is using. In Add a server the ones already taken are dimmed rather than withheld, so you can override the pick with any of the eight, including one already in use.


    
Trimmed

    
The test: a line earns its place if it changes what you would do. Reassurance, restating what is on screen, and explaining Smoozy's reasoning all fail it. About 40 places cut, most of them by half.

    
What went, by kind: reassurance ("always safe, whether the last attempt finished or not"), reasoning ("Smoozy restarts the server itself rather than stopping to ask — a setup that waited would leave it half-ready"), restating the obvious ("Right-click for the same actions"), and manual-writing in footers ("Order counts within one server only").

    
What stayed: anything carrying a number, a name, or a consequence. "Overrides noise threshold 0.01, time limit 30s, and FX's own 1024" is longer than most and earns every word.


    
Rules settled so far

    
    
      
  • Download and upload. The only words for moving a file.
    • 
      
  • Server for the rented one, your computer for yours. Never "machine".
    • 
      
  • A non-breaking space before every em dash. No orphans.
    • 
      
  • A number and its unit are never split across two lines: 47 GB, 240 frames.
    • 
      
  • All four are written into the whole-app Design document, Whole app, beside this file.
    • 
    


    
Conventions in the screens

    
    
      
  • Italic = the file's value. Upright bold = yours, with a cross beside it.
    • 
      
  • Blender's keyframe diamond for an animated View Layer. Solid = keyed on the read frame, hollow = not.
    • 
      
  • A pinned View Layer carries no diamond. The pin severs the file's animation, so the curve decides nothing.
    • 
      
  • Red field for a value that would be silently corrected.
    • 
      
  • Five endings. Four take a colour; the fifth is not an ending, so it is grey italic and the phrase carries the difference.
    • 
      
  • Two panels over a server, both collapsible to a strip. The check stays with its server.
    • 
      
  • A menu bar of four, holding only what has no other home. No File menu, no Undo, no Help.
    • 
      
  • A switch turns one thing on or off. A checkbox picks out of a set.
    • 
      
  • Settings holds only what belongs to your own computer or to the whole app. Never to one server.
    • 
    


    
About

    
The version, copyright, free-software notice and three links share the update box. Licence and Third-party licences open complete, selectable offline texts in this box; Close or Escape returns to About. Source code keeps About open. A refused request uses the ordinary failure shape. Donate appears only after an address is chosen.


    
The phone

    
Nothing here imitates Telegram. It is somebody else's app, so what is drawn is the shape of what Smoozy sends — bubbles, buttons under a message, a note pinned at the top — and the phone drawn around them carries no design decisions of its own.

    
Every message names its server. With one that is a formality; with three it is the only thing that makes one conversation readable.

    
One message per server, kept current rather than sent again, and it carries the moment it was last written. That moment is the whole mechanism behind a server going quiet: nothing is left to send that news, so a message that has not moved for twenty minutes is what the user reads instead.

    
On a rented container the Uptime line says unavailable, because the only figure that can be read there is the host's. It is drawn on Vast 5060 beside RunPod 4090, which has its own.

    
The pinned message names itself. It is Smoozy's own working note between the servers, and a pinned message nobody can make sense of and nobody can dismiss is worse than one that says what it is. Tapping it opens the rows; the first line says it is not for the user.

    
Every message Smoozy pins begins with a short, plainly readable head — the spec's own rule. Telegram writes a line into the conversation for every pin and that line quotes the pinned message from its start, and a phone keeps the current pin's first line in a banner at the top, so the head is all either surface has room for. The working note's head is the one drawn above: Smoozy — server coordination. The servers' own coordination messages are pinned too and take the same head with the server's name — Smoozy — server coordination · RunPod 4090 — so the line and the banner always read as Smoozy's own note rather than as machinery.

    
The seventeenth notes, 2026-10-23. Every job start has its own message, including a job sent at the desk. The single status message stays, edited on its existing clock and never pinned. Each later job message carries Stop this job; an album instead has its own short message immediately after it, since the live pass found that albums cannot carry buttons. Tapping Stop asks first and names that exact job and server; it never stops the next job. On an ended job it says the job has already ended. A waiting range asks whether to cancel the waiting job, with no claim that a frame is rendering.

    
The first-frame album and its question are separate. Every named copy of the check’s first frame is sent in its recorded order. The names drawn beneath the pictures stand for each picture’s caption: the recorded live pass found the phone shows it when the picture is opened, while the Mac shows the first caption under the album. The question follows at once, with Render all and Cancel bound to the held range job. Its Stop names that waiting range too. This keeps the existing every-layer rule and the album’s proven limit together. The ending sample still uses its existing main-copy rule (until 2026-10-31: a sheet for each View Layer, below). The Creator’s words, seventeenth note 4: “I need all the ones that were rendered on this first frame.” Sixteenth note 7: “I think maybe it should come with every message regarding a job. But probably with a verification message after the user clicks to avoid accidental stops.”


    
Everything after the head is a spoiler, and all of it arrives silently — Creator-stated, 2026-09-14. On the working note, on each server's own coordination message and on every other message the servers leave for each other, the head stays plain and the rest is blurred until it is tapped, so a person meets the head and a blur rather than machine content. Opening the pinned note keeps its head in view and shows the rows blurred; a tap on the blur shows them. Neither these messages nor their pins make the phone buzz. Nothing written for the user is blurred or silenced — the servers' running messages, frames, a finished job, a failure and every answer look exactly as they did.

    
The contact sheet is ten pictures, because a message holds ten. The sample is the first frame, the last, and eight spread evenly between them — of a 240-frame job the first ten would show four seconds of it.

    
A job of several View Layers gets a sheet for each, 2026-10-31. The same ten frames in each, the main View Layer’s sheet first and the others in the preview’s order, each naming its layer in its line: Living room — final · Reflections · 10 of 240 frames, evenly spread. A job of one View Layer gets one sheet with no name, as before. One sheet holding every layer was turned down: two layers would get five frames each and eleven would not fit at all, the reason a batch’s scenes each send their own. Drawn on A finished job of two View Layers: a sheet for each. The Creator, seventeenth note 10: “A Telegram message showing all frames at the end of the job only shows one view layer’s outputs.” Asked whether the sample should show every View Layer: “Yes to both your questions” (2026-10-30).

    
A failure carries three things, and the fourth waits for a tap. A plain sentence, what Smoozy recorded about whether the render printed anything at all, and a button. The render's own words carry the user's folder names, file paths and project names, and Telegram is a third party, so they stay on the server until the user taps for them.

    
The tap brings the words into the chat, readable there, and a file only when they do not fit — Creator-stated, 2026-09-14, after a text file on an Android phone needed another app to open. The server sends one ordinary message: a plain line naming the stream, then the words in a fixed-width block. Drawn on A job that failed is the fuller case. The three lines, to copy (the stream is Output or Errors, the desk's own tab names, and the job is its label):

    
— It fits whole: Output of Kitchen — final, in full. No file.
— It does not fit: Output of Kitchen — final, last 62 lines. Full log in the file below. The block holds the end, cut at a line, and the whole output follows as a file named Kitchen - final - Output.txt.
— The whole output is over 50 MB: Output of Kitchen — final, last 62 lines. Full log over 50 MB, too large to send. Open it in Smoozy on your computer. No file.

    
The file is a message of its own, directly under the block. An ordinary text message cannot carry a file, so with it means the next message. The cut is decided by length alone, and nothing in the block is picked out or explained. How Telegram wraps or scrolls a long line in the block is stated nowhere, so the drawing's wrapping is only there to keep it inside the phone.

    
Three of the five actions are a tap on the message in front of you — stopping the job, answering the first-frame check, and trying a failed job again — so nothing is typed and no server is named. The other two, status and frame 120, are typed, and where one leaves something open the answer is buttons rather than a question.

    
What the user asks for is the bot’s commands, 2026-10-31 — the Telegram discussion, Creator-stated: “Okay, so slash it is.” Typing / lists /status, /frame, /reporting and /stop, each with one line, and Telegram’s Menu button beside the message box opens the same list. No buttons stand under the message box: with nothing happening there is nothing to do from the phone. /frame alone sends the newest finished frame, since a command picked from the list arrives with no number; /stop asks Which job? where more than one is rendering or waiting. The old words, status and frame 120, still work. Drawn as Typing / lists the bot’s commands.

    
Reporting is one choice for every job from the phone, and the new default — Creator-stated the same day: “The choice … should apply to everything and be the new default.” /reporting offers the five choices the Render Settings list has, in its order, one a row; other minutes are typed. The reply says what was set and names only what did not take it. Settings’ radios are the same five, so the default can hold what the phone chose. Drawn as /reporting: one choice for every job and its reply.

    
Send a frame sits beside Stop this job on a rendering job’s own message, the runner’s take in that discussion, not objected to and drawn for the Creator’s look. One tap sends that job’s newest finished frame as a reply of its own; it is there only once a frame has finished. Drawn on both rendering servers’ messages, and as Send a frame beside Stop on a rendering job’s message.

    
The stop is on the two messages the user is looking at when they decide. The server's own running message, which is where somebody watching a render is; and a frame as it arrives, which is the moment the spec describes — a preview comes through, the render is plainly wrong, and it ends there instead of costing five more hours. It is the most valuable thing the phone offers, and it was drawn nowhere at all.

    
The label is Stop this job, which is the desk's own word for the act. One thing has one name in both places, and the spec's Stop it now names the choice rather than a button.

    
A failure on the phone takes the same shape as everywhere else — the red dot in front, the sentence in ordinary ink. It had been the other way round, the words red and no dot, which is the shape inverted. No cross: a recorded ending is not a condition, so there is nothing to clear.

    
Retry is drawn, and what the tap sends is not settled. The spec is firm that the button is offered on a failed job's message, so it is drawn without a mark on it. What that tap actually submits is another matter: submitting again opens the settings page precisely so the user changes something first, and a phone has no settings page. Rendering carries the open question and it is parked with the Creator — nothing here claims the tap and the page are the same act.

    
A job that writes a video sends the video, 2026-10-27 — the nineteenth notes, note 4, Creator-stated. Its start, its progress and its ending go as for any job; at a finished ending the video follows the finishing message as one video message, captioned with the job and the file’s name, where Telegram takes it (50 MB from a bot). The finishing message names the size either way, and where the video is bigger it says so and nothing follows it. A stopped or failed job sends no video, because what it leaves may not play.

    
A batch speaks once. Asking for every scene submits one job per scene, and the group says it is done once rather than twelve times, naming the group, the scenes and the frames in all. The contact sheet stays with its job. A message holds ten pictures, so one sheet spread across twelve scenes would show under one picture each and answer nothing — each scene sends its own as it finishes.

    
Its second line is two sentences rather than one. A lock allows the same three acts wherever they are asked for, but only two of them are on this screen: stopping and cancelling are a tap away, and downloading is done at the computer. The desk's band can list all three without misleading anybody; the phone cannot, so it says where the third one happens.

    
Telegram is switched on in Settings, and the bot is made there too, in a walkthrough that has nothing to choose: the two names ready to copy, another username on a tap, the whole reply pasted rather than the token picked out of it, and then the one thing Telegram makes the user do — press Start.

    
How much a job reports sits beside auto-download, on the submit strip, as a quiet line. A default is carried, so submitting normally asks nothing.


    
Starting a render, and starting it again

    
Rendering owns no screen, and that is on purpose. Submitting sits at the bottom of the settings panel; submitting again, and carrying on from where a job stopped, sit on a history entry. A third screen would describe no place.

    
Submitting is one button that names the count, and it asks nothing. Everything that could be confirmed is already on the page above it.

    
An all-scenes submission the connection broke gets three lists, not two. A scene has three endings — submitted, not submitted, and not known — and the third is only there while the connection is still down: once it comes back Smoozy reads the server before it names anything, so that row is gone. The offer is the remaining ones as a single act, so the user neither sends all twelve again nor sends the missing ones one at a time.

    
One event, one arithmetic. While four scenes are unknown the headline claims only what is confirmed — 5 of 12 scenes are confirmed submitted — and the offer carries no number at all. A count on that button would be counting the three Smoozy is sure about and quietly leaving out the four it is not, on a banner whose own third list says it cannot know. The counted label can come back when the connection does and the unknowns resolve.

    
Submitting again lands on the settings page, and the page says where its values came from. The convention here is that italic grey is the file's value and bold is the user's; on a re-submission the bold ones came out of an old job, and nothing else on the page would say so.

    
Two harder cases. With no server connected the page opens on the kept settings and waits: they are not lost because there is nowhere to submit them yet. With the job's own server gone the .blend has to be chosen again, so the file browser opens instead — on the server the user is already browsing, in the folder they are already in, because Smoozy picks no server and one is browsed at a time.

    
That bar says the file has to be found here, and that the folder it sat in on the old server means nothing on this one. Without it the user starts hunting a folder tree for a file that was never uploaded, which is the work this whole case exists to save them. It does not say whether the file is up there: Smoozy has not looked, and hunting through somebody's own files for them is not something this app does.

    
Carrying on is the same page with one difference, so the band is where that difference is said. The range has moved, and the band names the frame it moved to and where that frame came from — the last frame with a file written on the server. The figure is read from the server when the action is taken, and the band carries the spec's own limit beside it: a file that is short but not empty still counts as finished, so a frame the server stopped part-way through can be counted as finished and left out. The band never claims the frame is finished — that is a claim the reckoning cannot make; and where the server answers but its outputs cannot be read, the band says that instead and names the frame the entry recorded. A remembered figure is never presented as a checked one. Either way the range is still the user's to type over.

    
Simplify shows its three settings once the switch is on — Max Subdivision, Child Particles and Texture Limit, under Blender's own names, because those are the names an artist already knows. Three greyed rows above an off switch would be three things to read past. Two things in that group are deliberately absent: Texture Resolution, which only one of the four supported Blenders has and would appear and disappear with the Blender chosen; and the two culling settings, which drop whole objects out of the frame — a far larger change to somebody's picture than a coarser mesh or a smaller texture.

    
The switch and the three take the page's own composition — the file's read-back value in the file's italic, the user's answer in bold with the cross that hands the file's value back. A saved scene records Simplify's switch and a pair of values for each of the three, all readable back like anything else, so there is a file value behind every row. No starting value is invented: the drawn 2, 0.50 and 1024 this note once defended came from no document and are gone. Without pre-filled reducing values the offer starts at the file's own limits, which on an untouched scene may cut little — a recorded cost, not an oversight.

    
A file saved with Simplify already on is an ordinary case, not an edge. It renders as the artist saved it: the switch shows the file's state, the offer gives way to a statement of the file's own setting, and nothing forces a saved switch off — that would un-match a picture from its own file.

    
A stop Smoozy stopped waiting for says only what it knows — Stop sent. Timed out waiting for the render to end.. It cannot tell a stop that failed from a render slow to honour it, so it claims neither, the entry corrects itself when the outcome arrives, and a new stop can be sent.


    
When something goes wrong

    
One shape wherever a failure attaches. A red dot, one plain sentence saying what did not happen, a second sentence only where Smoozy actually knows what to do about it, then the controls: whatever act would try again, the raw text where there is any, and a cross that clears it. The thing it sits on decides how much room it has, never what it is made of. Exactly two additions are permitted anywhere and no more: a box the user is standing in front of may offer the act they came to do, beside the retry, so a failure in the middle of something does not trap them; and reporting, which is below.

    
The cross is only on a failure that is still true. A connection that is down and a folder that refused a write are conditions: the user clears them, or they clear themselves when the condition ends. A failed job carries no cross — freeing the disk does not put back the frames that were never rendered, so the record stands and there is nothing to clear.

    
One panel shows what the machine printed, opened from every Blender output and every What the server said. They all show the same kind of thing, so there is one of it rather than one per screen. The control names whose text it is, which is also why there is no single word for both.

    
A render has two streams and they stay apart, so it has two tabs: Output and Errors. Each has its own record and they can differ — the output collected in full while the errors were only partly recorded is an ordinary case. Anything with one stream has no tabs.

    
The panel never shows an empty box. Four things a tab's record can be — and a fifth that is none of them, where the server ran out of room to write the outcome down. It says which: the text; Blender wrote nothing here, in that stream's own words; partly recorded, with how much was kept and why the rest went; and no output was recorded. That is the architecture's closed set, one outcome per stream rather than one per render, and none of the four is an empty box. The last two are different facts, and a user who cannot tell them apart learns nothing from either.

    
So the two tabs can hold two different outcomes at once, and on one ending they do. Where the machine's own memory ran out, Errors came back empty and Output did not — the render printed on to a sampling line and stopped there. Open a render that ended without complaining and switch tabs: the sentence is on one side and the render's own lines are on the other. Nothing is lifted out of those lines, not even the last one, because setting a line of the ordinary output under the plain sentence would name a cause by placement that Smoozy does not have.

    
This said the opposite until 2026-09-02, and it is worth leaving on the page as the shape of the fault: it read a render that printed nothing at all is answered on the entry instead — no control and no panel. The render had printed plenty; only the complaints stream was empty. Taking the control away avoided the blank box by removing the sentence that answers the user's question, which is the thing the spec was written to prevent.

    
Nothing is trimmed and nothing is explained. Smoozy does not try to work out why from this text. The meaning is in the plain sentence on the thing that failed, and where Smoozy is guessing there is no second sentence.

    
No Save and no Copy. No spec grants either, the text is selectable, and the menu bar already carries copy.

    
A failure can be reported to the Creator from where it sits. Report a problem…, after the raw text and before the cross, and quiet — the retry stays the loud one, because a connection dropping when you shut your laptop is the commonest failure in the app and is nobody’s bug. This is the second addition the failure shape permits, and the last. A failure collapsed onto one line of a list does not carry it, for the same reason it carries no raw text: the row has no room, and both wait for the surface it opens onto.

    
And after a crash Smoozy raises it itself, at the next launch. The one time a failure appears somewhere other than on the thing that failed, granted as a named exception. Its most important line is that nothing was lost — a crash and a clean close leave Smoozy in the same state, so a box saying only did not close properly would frighten somebody about work that is perfectly safe.

    
It asks only about a crash it has not already asked about. There is no way to switch the prompt off and that stands — it is the one moment Smoozy is allowed to speak up about a failure that is on no screen. But a version that goes out with a real bug crashes on most runs, and a box in the middle of the screen at every launch all week is nagging, which is past where Smoozy's job stops. Asking once about each crash removes that without adding a setting for the user to manage. (Ruled 2026-09-02.)

    
The report box says only what is true at each moment. Where the system names no downloads folder, nothing is proposed: No folder chosen, and Save report asks for a folder first. While the report is prepared, which can mean reading the server, Save report is underway and nothing claims a file yet. Where the folder did not open, the box names the file and its folder and says the folder could not be opened, rather than saying it did. (Drawn 2026-10-24.)

    
Escape collapses a panel, and a panel's work is never stopped by a key. Escape closes whatever is on top, and for a panel that means the strip that keeps counting rather than an ending — so a dependency check that has been running for minutes survives it. Stopping something stays a deliberate act with a control behind it, because one mistaken keypress should not be able to discard work that took minutes. (Ruled 2026-09-02; it had been unstated whether the two were the same act.)


    
Showing that something is underway

    
Three shapes, and what the user can still do decides which. On the control, where the control they pressed is the thing working and the rest of the screen still works — it keeps its place and its width, loses its label, and is unavailable until it finishes. On the row, where the work belongs to one row of a list they will come back to. Over the pane, where nothing on that pane can be used until it finishes.

    
Where two look possible, the narrowest that is true wins, because a shape that covers more than it has to takes away work the user could have been doing.

    
One thing never carries two of them. A server Smoozy is repairing already says so on its row, so its Connect control keeps its amber — which is state rather than an underway mark — and what it does not additionally do is lose its label or spin. (This said the control was “left alone” until 2026-09-02, which read as it carrying nothing at all, when in fact it is already carrying its own state.)

    
Anything underway also says how far along, or says it cannot say. A spinner that never becomes a figure is the app admitting it does not know, which is fair to admit and not fair to leave unsaid.


    
Notifications, and updating

    
The operating system draws a notification, so only two things here are ours — what each one says, and what clicking it does. Clicking brings Smoozy forward and opens the thing it is about: a job's entry, a server's row. It goes where the user would have had to go anyway, so none of them is a dead end.

    
A finished job says two figures, how many frames and how long, because those are what a user wants before deciding whether to go and look. A failure names where it stopped and nothing about why — what Smoozy knows about the cause is on the entry, and a notification is not a place to start reading.

    
The finished-job switch in Settings no longer promises the frame outright. The picture is absent four ways that are none of them faults: too large for the system to attach, dropped by a system that gives no signal, refused by a system whose own pages contradict each other, or not on this computer yet at the moment of posting. So it reads with the frame, where the job has one.

    
Updating shows nothing at all on Mac and Windows. Smoozy fetches and installs, and the next start is the new version. No announcement, nothing asked, and no list of what changed — the promise is that updating is not something to think about, and a message about it is thinking about it.

    
Nothing is installed while a job is running or a transfer is under way, on any system — a job waiting in line or on the user's answer counts. The new version waits and goes in by itself once nothing is running. About is where the user can install it anyway: the new-version line says it is waiting, and Install now sits under one sentence saying what that does — Smoozy restarts, jobs keep rendering on their servers, uploads and downloads stop. It is a form of the new-version reading, not a fifth one. On the Creator's ruling of 2026-09-28.

    
On Linux there is one box, once per version. A new version arrives as a package, installing one needs the computer password, and the system draws that request. Smoozy says what it is for first, because a password box arriving out of nowhere is a thing a user is right to refuse. Not now is not a failure: they stay on the version they have, and nothing asks again until the next one arrives.

    
A new version that could not start is said on Linux, and so is the way back. Where the system will not let Smoozy put the previous version back without asking, that box is all the window shows; the system asks only once Reinstall is pressed, and a declined or failed attempt says Reinstall failed. in the same box. Smoozy went quiet at both moments before (step 11 D6b, 2026-10-26).

    
Check for updates stays, on the Creator's ruling. It was taken out earlier the same day on the belief that no spec gave the user an update action, and put back on the Creator’s ruling — and the belief was wrong as well as overruled: Preparation/Specs/Whole app.md grants the user the act outright, written in on 2026-08-25. It does its work in About, which is where the version already lives and where an update is the only thing that ever surfaces — four readings in one box: the version and when it was last checked, Checking…, a new version found, and a check that could not be reached. About is also the only thing in the app that names the version, which matters because Smoozy updates itself and says nothing.

    
Being asked for a password

    
One dialog, and it names the step that was refused rather than asking for a password out of nowhere. The three choices for how long Smoozy keeps it sit under the field, because that is the moment the user is deciding it.

    
Where the computer has nowhere to keep a password, only the choice to remember it for good is absent — not greyed out, and not all three. The architecture composes the offer from what the computer can do: asking each time and keeping it while this connection lasts both work without a store, so both stay.

    
A system's own question is the system's, and Smoozy draws none of it. A Mac may ask whether Smoozy may still read what it remembered on three occasions — after the user updates their system, after Smoozy updates itself, or if Smoozy has been changed on the computer — and it does not happen every time. All three, and the sometimes, are Apple's own; drawing one occasion would have a user meet the dialog twice more with no account of why. When the answer is no, Smoozy does not ask for the password: the system still holds it, so asking would have the user retype a secret that is not lost. The dialog reports that the system would not hand it back, keeps it remembered, and offers the step again. It asks only where nothing was remembered.


    
Resizing a pane

    
Every seam between two panes drags — the rail, a list against its entry, and a job entry's main column against its preview. Try it. A desktop application whose panes are a fixed size reads as a web page, which is the first thing this design decided against.

    
Each pane stops at the smallest width that is still useful, so none of them can be dragged into nothing and then have to be hunted for.

    
The narrowing steps still win underneath. Set the rail wide, then take the window down to 720 on the bar below: the rail goes to badges, because that is the app's decision about what fits rather than the user's. Take the window back up and the width you set is still there.

    
Double-click a seam to put it back. That is the only reset there is.

    
One width, not one per screen. The rail is on every screen, so its width is the same on all of them; a list's width is the same for the queue and history, which are the same shape of screen.


    
The eighteenth notes

    
A stopped setup says its failure once, on the step, as one line with What the server said at its end, and Server output sits under the steps once its window has gone. Ten steps line up by their point.

    
Nothing is silent while a setup runs. Smoozy's own program prints its download and unpack progress like a terminal downloader, both streams show in the window, and a line still being written shows as far as it has got.

    
A dependency row already uploading says so, and Upload counts only the rest. Frames read as they were typed, in Queue and History. The large preview fills the window. The frame row is compact. Removed servers' jobs sit in one folding group at the foot of History, with their own clearing box. A message about an ended job carries no Stop.


    
Walking it

    
The screens are joined up. The rail and the menus go where they say; a server opens; a .blend brings up its settings; submitting lands in the queue; sending a file's missing pieces lands in Transfers; right-clicking a file gives that file's menu.

    
A control with nothing drawn behind it says so, at the bottom of the window. That is there so a walk through shows where the holes are.
